title: Draw the AWS Global Infrastructure
description: Describe the relationship between Regions, AZs, and Edge Locations.
problemStatement:
In your own words, describe the hierarchy of AWS global infrastructure. Include:
- What is a Region?
- What is an Availability Zone (AZ)?
- What is an Edge Location?
- How do they relate to each other (e.g., how many AZs per Region)?

Use a simple analogy (e.g., countries, cities, post offices) to make your explanation clear.
hints: A Region is a physical geographical area with multiple isolated data centres.
AZs are those isolated data centres within a Region – usually at least two.
Edge Locations are different; they are caching endpoints for CloudFront, not compute resources.
expectedOutput: A written description that correctly defines all three terms and shows the relationship, plus an analogy.
solutionCode: AWS operates a global network of data centres organised into Regions. A Region is a named geographical area (like us-east-1 in Northern Virginia) that contains at least two Availability Zones. Each Availability Zone consists of one or more discrete data centres with independent power, cooling, and networking, connected by fast private fibre. This isolation means if one AZ goes down, applications running in another AZ stay available. Edge Locations are separate from Regions and AZs; they are sites used by Amazon CloudFront to cache copies of content closer to end users. Using the city analogy: a Region is like a city, AZs are separate secure buildings within that city, and Edge Locations are like neighbourhood delivery lockers scattered around the world.
